claims.text: The base alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing about 1 wt.% oxygen matches available experimental conditions and represents realistic defect content.
The proposed framework will explicitly separate phonon and electronic heat transport while incorporating defects.
The framework will predict total thermal conductivity from 100 to 1200 K within ±15% of measurements.
The framework will outperform traditional single-parameter or perfect-crystal models.
The model will couple ab initio phonon and electron calculations with separate lattice and electronic transport measurements and explicit defect configurations.
Oxygen incorporation and chemical disorder strongly modify phonon-scattering channels in BCC HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen incorporation and chemical disorder strongly modify the alloy's electronic states.
The effects of oxygen and chemical disorder necessitate explicit decoupling of lattice and electronic conduction.
Accounting separately for local chemical fluctuations, lattice distortions, and defect scattering for phonons and electrons will capture interactions missed by standard treatments.
Treatments based on a single Debye temperature or perfect-crystal assumptions miss relevant cross-interactions.
Predictive accuracy will improve by at least 10–15% relative to earlier models.
The framework will consistently predict separate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity components across 100–1200 K.
Previous simplified or defect-free models predict total conductivity of approximately 10–17 W/(m·K) from 300 to 1200 K.
Previous models do not fully resolve phonon and electron contributions or oxygen-doping effects.
The stated applicability domain is single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than about 1 wt.% oxygen between 100 and 1200 K.
Above 1 wt.% oxygen or 1200 K, additional phases or transport mechanisms may reduce predictive fidelity.
Thermal diffusivity and specific-heat measurements can be used to obtain the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution.
Electrical-resistivity measurements can be used to estimate the electronic contribution and thereby partition total thermal conductivity.
The hypothesis is falsified if either partial contribution differs from measurement by more than ±20%, or total conductivity differs by more than ±15%, at any tested temperature from 100 to 1200 K.
